m31.name: Andromeda Galaxy
m31.note: The nearest large spiral, about 2.5 million light-years away and visible to the naked eye; it is closing on the Milky Way at roughly 110 km/s.

m51.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
m51.note: The first galaxy recognised as a spiral, by Lord Rosse in 1845; it is gravitationally entangled with its small companion NGC 5195.

m104.name: Sombrero Galaxy
m104.note: Found by Pierre Méchain in 1781, its bright bulge crossed by a thick dust lane gives the brim-and-crown outline that earned its name.

m87.name: M87
m87.note: A giant elliptical at the heart of the Virgo Cluster; its black hole M87* was the first ever imaged, by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.

lmc.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
lmc.note: A satellite of the Milky Way visible to the naked eye from the south; supernova SN 1987A, the nearest seen since 1604, erupted here in 1987.

centaurusA.name: Centaurus A
centaurusA.note: The nearest radio galaxy, recorded by James Dunlop in 1826; jets from its black hole feed radio lobes hundreds of thousands of light-years across.

m42.name: Orion Nebula
m42.note: The nearest massive star-forming region, about 1,344 light-years away and visible to the naked eye; the Trapezium cluster lights it from within.

m1.name: Crab Nebula
m1.note: Remnant of the supernova seen by Chinese and Japanese observers in 1054; its pulsar spins about 30 times a second, and it is Messier's first entry.

m57.name: Ring Nebula
m57.note: A planetary nebula found by Antoine Darquier in 1779; the shed outer layers of a dying Sun-like star form a ring around its white-dwarf core.

ngc7293.name: Helix Nebula
ngc7293.note: One of the closest planetary nebulae, about 655 light-years away, discovered by Karl Ludwig Harding around 1824.

carina.name: Carina Nebula
carina.note: A vast southern nebula recorded by Lacaille in 1752, larger than the Orion Nebula and home to Eta Carinae, one of the most massive stars known.

m16.name: Eagle Nebula
m16.note: Home of the Pillars of Creation, the star-forming columns photographed by the Hubble Space Telescope in 1995, where new stars are still being born.

m45.name: Pleiades
m45.note: An open cluster about 444 light-years away whose six or seven naked-eye stars appear in Homer and the Bible; its Japanese name is Subaru.

m13.name: Hercules Cluster
m13.note: A globular cluster found by Edmond Halley in 1714; in 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message toward it for any listening civilisation.

omegaCentauri.name: Omega Centauri
omegaCentauri.note: The largest and brightest globular cluster in the Milky Way, holding some 10 million stars; Ptolemy listed it as a single star.

hyades.name: Hyades
hyades.note: The nearest open cluster to the Sun, forming the V of the Bull's face; bright Aldebaran at its tip is a much closer foreground star, not a member.

sgrA.name: Sagittarius A*
sgrA.note: The Milky Way's central supermassive black hole, about 4 million solar masses; tracking stars around it earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

cygnusX1.name: Cygnus X-1
cygnusX1.note: An X-ray source found in 1964, the first object widely accepted as a black hole; Stephen Hawking conceded his bet with Kip Thorne over it in 1990.

velaPulsar.name: Vela Pulsar
velaPulsar.note: Found in 1968, it spins every 89 milliseconds inside the remnant of a supernova 11,000 years ago and is one of the brightest gamma-ray sources.

quasar3c273.name: 3C 273
quasar3c273.note: The first quasar identified, when Maarten Schmidt read its redshift in 1963; still the brightest quasar in our sky, its light 2.4 billion years old.

betelgeuse.name: Betelgeuse
betelgeuse.note: Orion's red supergiant, large enough to reach Jupiter's orbit if placed at the Sun; its Great Dimming of 2019–2020 was visible to the naked eye.

proxima.name: Proxima Centauri
proxima.note: The Sun's nearest stellar neighbour, a red dwarf found by Robert Innes in 1915; the planet Proxima b was confirmed in its habitable zone in 2016.

vega.name: Vega
vega.note: The first star after the Sun to be photographed, at Harvard in 1850; Earth's axial precession makes it the pole star again in about 12,000 years.

sirius.name: Sirius
sirius.note: The night sky's brightest star, 8.6 light-years away; its companion Sirius B, seen by Alvan Clark in 1862, was among the first known white dwarfs.

lineage.intro: Your hydrogen came from the Big Bang, your carbon and oxygen from the cores of stars, your iron from supernovae and your gold from colliding neutron stars
